tone_statements.citation: Krauss, Michael E. 1979. Athabaskan Tone. Typescript, Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska, Fairbanks, October 1979, 72 pp. (first draft August 1978; 2003 retyped version). Alaska Native Language Archive item CA961K1978.
tone_statements.quote: Although Boas is not explicitly aware of any Tsetsaut tone, he uses an acute accent mark impressionistically where he hears stress. The accent mark tends to fall on the last syllable of the word most of the time. [...] However, when the accent mark is not written on the last syllable, it is almost always on a non-constricted syllable, not a preceding constricted syllable. [...] The most probable explanation of this inconsistency is that besides phonetic stress on the last syllable, there may well have been low pitch from constricted vowels, high from non-constricted, as in Tahltan and the other low-marked languages. [...] There are, however, enough counterexamples [...] to cast some doubt on this interpretation.
tone_statements.locator: typescript (2003 retyping) pp. 59-60, section 7.1 'Extinct Athabaskan' (= Krauss 2005 section 7.1, within CILT 269 pp. 55-136)
tone_statements.summary: Probable (explicitly tentative) low-marked tone: constricted (PA glottalic) stem vowels low, non-constricted high, Tahltan-type, inferred from the distribution of Boas's accent marks, alongside phonetic word-final stress; Krauss notes counterexamples and calls the reading provisional.

sources.citation: Boas, Franz & Pliny Earle Goddard. 1924. Ts'ets'aut, an Athapascan language from Portland Canal, British Columbia. International Journal of American Linguistics 3(1): 1-35.
sources.note: Short phonetics discussion (pp. 2-4) covers the labial shift and loss of final consonants; on accent Goddard writes only 'The first thing to suggest itself is accent, but what do we know of that?' (p. 3). Boas's phonetic key (p. 2 fn. 1) defines vowels, consonants, glottal stop and length but no accent symbol; the vocabulary nonetheless carries acute/prime accent marks on forms. No rule for stress placement is stated.

sources.citation: Boas, Franz. 1895. Fifth report on the Indians of British Columbia. In: Tenth report on the north-western tribes of Canada, Report of the 65th meeting of the British Association for the Advancement of Science (Ipswich 1895) [CIHM microfiche 14342]; section '2. The Ts'ets'a'ut', report pp. 66-67, plus alphabet key at front.
sources.note: Grammar notes (noun, numerals, pronouns, verb paradigms) with accent-marked transcriptions (e.g. etlie'e, tloky'ada'); Boas says only 'Tinneh phonetics are difficult, and Levi could not be induced to speak slowly'. The report's alphabet key defines '!' as 'increased stress of articulation' (a consonant diacritic), nothing on word accent. No stress statement.

sources.locator: typescript (2003 retyping) pp. 59-60, section 7.1 'Extinct Athabaskan' (= Krauss 2005 section 7.1, within CILT 269 pp. 55-136)
sources.note: The only explicit discussion of Tsetsaut prosody in the literature. Krauss reads Boas's impressionistic acute accents: they mostly fall on the word-final syllable (phonetic final stress), but when non-final they sit almost always on non-constricted rather than constricted syllables, which he takes as probable evidence of low-marked tone (low pitch from constricted vowels, high from non-constricted, as in Tahltan); he lists supporting forms and counterexamples and leaves the interpretation explicitly tentative pending fuller identification of Boas's forms. Contrasts Tsetsaut with Kwalhioqua-Tl…
